extracted.intended_audience: general public, researchers and stakeholders interested in global health financing and the Global Fund's operations
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of The Global Fund's purpose, funding model, governance structures, oversight mechanisms, and operational procedures for allocating and managing grants to fight HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis and malaria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Country Coordinating Mechanism (CCM) composition requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Country Coordinating Mechanisms, country-level committees consisting of in-country stakeholders that need to include, according to Global Fund requirements, a broad spectrum of representatives from government, NGOs, faith-based organizations, the private sector, and people living with the diseases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to oversee implementation in-country; model aims to ensure broad stakeholder representation but the page notes concerns about conflict of interest because some stakeholders on CCMs may also be grant recipients, sub-recipients, contractors or paid participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding on the basis of performance (original objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: The initial objective of the Global Fund – to provide funding to countries on the basis of performance – was supposed to make it different from other international agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five-year evaluation in 2009 concluded that without a standing body of technical staff the Fund could not ascertain actual results and therefore tended to use disbursements or purchase of inputs as proxies for performance; implies a requirement/expectation that funding decisions be tied to measurable achievement against agreed indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-year allocation and replenishment cycle (New Funding Model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under this funding model, eligible countries receive an allocation of money every three years for possible use during the same three-year period. The total amount of all allocations across all countries depends on the amount contributed by governments and other donors through the 'replenishment' fundraising during the same three-year period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replenishment conferences are held to raise multi-year pledges; country allocations and grant planning are structured around these three-year cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application process and Principal Recipient (PR) selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The countries, through their Country Coordinating Mechanism (CCM), submit applications outlining how they will use the allocation, including selecting the main implementers of grants in countries called Principal Recipients (PR) to carry about programs within their respective countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications must name PRs; selection transparency and appropriateness of PRs are material to grant approval and later program performance and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent Technical Review Panel (TRP) review
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent Technical Review Panel (TRP) reviews the applications and there will be an iterative process towards the finalisation of the applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TRP provides technical appraisal and requests iterations; TRP independence is a core part of the application approval standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding disbursement tied to agreed indicators and actual expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the applications are approved, the Global Fund provides funding to the principal recipients based on achievement toward agreed indicators and actual expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This operationalizes the performance-based intent: disbursements are conditioned on indicator achievement and expense justification; local monitoring and verification are used to assess progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Fund Agent (LFA) periodic review role
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance and expenses are periodically reviewed by a 'local fund agent', which in most countries is an international financial audit company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LFAs act as in-country financial/monitoring agents to verify performance and expenditures and inform disbursement decisions; weaknesses in LFAs or oversight have been flagged in past reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board composition and constituency representation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board includes 20 voting members, with equal representation by implementers and donors. Non-governmental organisations; communities living with and/or affected by HIV, TB and malaria; the private sector; and private foundations are also represented as voting members. There are also eight non-voting members, including the board chair and vice-chair; representatives of partner organisations including the World Health Organization and World Bank; as well as the Additional Public Donors constituency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board structure is intended to embody the partnership approach; equal implementer/donor representation and inclusion of affected communities are explicit governance criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board core functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The core functions of the Board include: strategy development; governance oversight; commitment of financial resources; assessment of organisational performance; risk management; and partnership engagement, resource mobilisation and advocacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated functions set expectations for Board responsibilities and performance in steering the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board committee structure and constituency representation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of the Board operates through three committees where each constituency should be represented in at least one standing committee, which are the Audit and Finance Committee (AFC), Ethics and Governance Committee (EGC), and the Strategy Committee (SC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee membership rules aim to ensure that all constituencies have representation within Board-level oversight and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office of the Inspector General (OIG) independence and anti-corruption role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Global Fund Office of the Inspector General – an auditing unit independent from the Global Fund Secretariat – conducts audits and investigations; the Fund states it has 'zero tolerance for corruption and actively seeks to uncover any evidence of misuse of its funds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIG findings have detailed fraud and misuse; the OIG's independence, investigation processes, and reporting are central accountability mechanisms. The page notes controversies (e.g., dismissal of OIG head) that raise questions about protection of that independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoveries and sanctions policy for misappropriated funds
rubrics_metrics.description: After pushing countries to reclaim stolen funds from the parties responsible and recovering only about half, the organization began in 2014 as a last resort reducing future grants by twice the amount of misappropriated funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing future grants is a remedial/sanctioning approach; the OIG audited the recoveries process in 2020. Recovery and sanction practices are part of fiduciary risk management and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and procurement/selection standards for applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: The Global Fund rejected Kenya's application for US$114 million due to a lack of transparency in the selection of firms to manage the fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent procurement and selection processes for fund managers/implementers are treated as material eligibility/quality criteria for grant approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest risk from stakeholder representation and partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: The model has raised concerns about conflict of interest, as some of the stakeholders represented on the Country Coordinating Mechanisms may also receive money from the Global Fund, either as grant recipients, sub-recipients, private persons (e.g. for travel or participation at seminars) or contractors. The partnership with Heineken was criticized as a conflict of interest undermining health objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflict-of-interest management is implicit in governance rules and in controversy responses; partnerships and stakeholder roles are scrutinized against public health objectives and perceptions of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and administrative status constraints (U.S. law example)
rubrics_metrics.description: From January 2006, while being a 501(c)(3) organization, it received status under International Organizations Immunities Act in the United States. Per law in the United States, funding for the Global Fund cannot exceed one-third of total contributions from all donors to the Global Fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal status affects privileges and limitations (e.g., contribution ceilings under U.S. law) and has operational and fundraising implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational distinction: financing mechanism vs implementing agency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Global Fund is a financing mechanism rather than an implementing agency. Programs are implemented by in-country partners such as ministries of health, while the Global Fund secretariat ... monitor the programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction shapes expectations about the Fund's role, staffing (secretariat housed in Geneva only), reliance on partners, and limits on direct technical engagement; it underscores why standards for partner selection, monitoring, and verification are crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for technical capacity to measure program results
rubrics_metrics.description: Without a standing body of technical staff, the Global Fund is not able to ascertain the actual results of its projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied standard: adequate technical capacity (either in-house or through partners) is necessary to verify results beyond inputs/disbursements. The page records this as an evaluative finding and a criterion for credible performance-based financing.
